participants: Chris Klevan (sales manager, ran the meeting)
Andrew Musial (closer, appears in diarization as 'Andrew Jin (Primal Instinct)')
Derek Harris (new hire, introduced on this call)
summary: Sixty-four-minute daily sales team meeting run by Chris Klevan: introductions for a new hire, wins round, weekly projections, then two live role-play training blocks. Derek Harris was introduced as a new team member — 22, based in Virginia, prior experience 'between setting and closing, mostly setting', brought in through a mutual friend of Chris's. The projections segment ran cash and unit targets per rep (Kim at 10 sets needing two more, Andrew at 12K needing two more paid-in-full deals, Richard behind). The first role-play had Richard running discovery on Chris playing a well-conditioned, low-pain 'optimizer' prospect; Chris's coaching was that consequence questions do not work on someone already committed and consistent, that the frame should be 'the cost of staying good' rather than the cost of inaction, and that reps must not invent pain — 'You're not here to create something that isn't there. You're here to be a mirror to what is.' The second block was Andrew practising the price drop, at his own request, because payment and price objection handling is 'the thing that comes up for me the most that I [mess] up with'. He failed it in the way he had just named: given a think-about-it plus a $200-a-month expectation, he isolated finances and moved to structuring payment rather than testing value. Chris diagnosed it explicitly — 'You were trying to figure out the logistics. And I was trying to tell you, I don't care about logistics... I don't see the value that it's worth $6,000' — and taught that wanting to shop around is a value objection, not a money one.
notable: Derek Harris is introduced as a brand-new team member on this date: 22 years old, in Virginia, 'I've worked on a couple of different offers, like between setting and closing, mostly setting though', recruited via 'kind of a mutual friend of me and Chris'. He is a candidate identity for the unresolved 'DH' setter code in the title suffixes — but only for calls dated on or after 2026-07-07. Any DH-suffixed call before this date cannot be him.

A $200-a-month product is treated as an established fallback, not an improvisation. In the role-play Chris voiced the prospect's expectation — 'I expected it was going to be, like, a $200-a-month thing, I didn't really know what this was' — and Richard immediately answered 'I can still run you through the 2-on-in-a-month thing, see if you're interested in that, yeah', with no correction from the manager. On the same day, roughly ninety minutes after this meeting, Andrew Musial ran exactly that move live on the Luke Charleston call, dropping from $6,000 to a $200/month Skool tier.

Andrew was coached on his price-objection failure mode at 18:07 and reproduced it on a live call at 19:41 the same evening. In this role-play he asked 'is it more matter of, it's actually tight right now? Or, you could probably do it?' instead of testing value, and was corrected. On the Luke Charleston call he skipped the financial questions entirely and went straight to a cheaper product. This meeting is the single best piece of evidence that the gap is known, named and unclosed.

Chris's own framing of the offer to the team: 'because this is a transformation program, it's super premium. And so it's not usually something that people just, like, out of the blue do in a lot of cases. It's not, like, a need or a necessity. It's definitely something that people do as a luxury to make sure that they achieve the results that they're looking for.'

Chris coaches active disqualification when there is no real goal: 'let me send you a video that goes over everything... But right now, it just doesn't seem like it makes any sense because honestly, for you to spend thousands of dollars on coaching like this right now, like, I don't really think it would make sense for you.' Andrew endorsed it — 'Sometimes it's better to just dig that out to the surface than trying to artificially manufacture a need in someone when actually there is no need.' This is a healthy stated norm and is worth measuring against actual behaviour on the calls.

Richard voiced the opposite instinct and was corrected in the room. Richard: 'you still have to make it look big enough for them in order to actually have them.' Chris: 'You can't make something look big enough that isn't there. So you have to look at what is there. And you got to be honest.'

Kim reported a prospect who came to kettlebells through Trevor's free content after a motorcycle accident in which 'both wrists got completely reconstructed', who cannot invest now for custody reasons and will 'save up for 90 days'. Chris's response: 'we got to get that guy in the program.' Nobody was sold anything on that call, but it is the second reconstructive-surgery case surfacing in this batch's orbit and no clinical screening was mentioned.

Reps are coached to disclaim expertise if challenged: 'Your trainer's Trevor. Like, I'm just here to help see if it's a good fit. And Trevor trained me specifically to see if somebody's a good fit for the program or not. I'm not your actual coach.' Chris adds 'I'm also here to keep the people that are jerks away from the program.'

Projections vocabulary for the rollup: 'sets' (setter bookings), 'units' (deals), 'PIFs' (paid in full). Andrew's target as stated: 'You need two more PIFs for the cash.' Andrew's stated cadence: 'I only have two days because I'm, you know, deal a day.'
